One of the most contentious issues surrounding this era is the number of casualties that occurred during the campaign. While some sources estimate that millions of people died as a result of the Great Leap Forward, others argue that the actual number of casualties was significantly lower.

The Great Leap Forward was a massive effort to transform China's economy from an agrarian society to an industrial one. The campaign involved the forced collectivization of farms, the establishment of communes, and the rapid industrialization of the country. However, the ambitious goals and the methods used to achieve them led to widespread suffering and hardship.

The famine was caused by a combination of factors, including poor agricultural policies, natural disasters, and the disruption of traditional farming practices. The official Chinese government has long maintained that the famine resulted in the deaths of 36 million people, but this figure has been widely disputed.

Some scholars have suggested that the true number of deaths was closer to 1 million, while others have proposed even lower estimates.

The debate over the number of casualties in the Great Leap Forward is complex and multifaceted.
